analysis.investment_thesis: Neochem Bio trades at INR 71.90 against a Graham Number of ~INR 37, implying a 95% premium to intrinsic value — precisely the opposite of the margin of safety I require. With debt-to-equity of 1.8x and a price-to-book of 5.85x, the market is pricing in a growth story I am not willing to pay for.
key_strengths: Revenue compounding strongly: 48→61→84 Cr (~32% CAGR), with operating income tripling to 13 Cr in 2025
Promoter holding at 66.7% with meaningful DII interest (13.2%) suggests some institutional conviction
Earnings positive for all 3 years (1→2→8 Cr net profit), clearing my minimum earnings continuity test
key_risks: Debt-to-equity of 1.8x (36 Cr borrowings vs 20 Cr equity) — far exceeds my 0.5x ceiling; finance costs consuming 4 Cr of 13 Cr operating income
Price-to-book of 5.85x (117 Cr market cap vs 20 Cr equity) — I never pay this kind of premium over net assets
Free cash flow barely turned positive in 2025 (1 Cr) after two negative years; OCF of 3 Cr is dangerously thin versus 36 Cr in debt obligations
red_flags: Graham Number ~INR 37 vs market price INR 71.90 — stock is nearly 100% above its quantitative fair value
Interest coverage ratio of 3.25x (13 Cr EBIT / 4 Cr finance cost) — below my 3.5x minimum safety threshold
No dividend history disclosed — retained earnings are being consumed by debt service, not returned to shareholders
Tiny absolute scale: INR 117 Cr market cap on INR 8 Cr net profit leaves zero margin for operational error
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Neochem Bio fails on virtually every quantitative filter I have established over decades of security analysis. The price-to-book ratio of 5.85x is the most damning: I am being asked to pay INR 5.85 for every rupee of net assets, in a specialty chemicals business with no demonstrated competitive moat and a balance sheet carrying INR 36 Cr of borrowings against INR 20 Cr of equity. My Graham Number computation — the square root of (22.5 × EPS of ~4.91 × BVPS of ~12.28) — yields approximately INR 37, against which the current price of INR 71.90 represents a near-100% speculative premium. That premium belongs to the seller, not the buyer.

The 2025 profit jump to INR 8 Cr from INR 2 Cr is notable but suspect as a basis for valuation: operating cash flow is only INR 3 Cr and free cash flow barely positive at INR 1 Cr, suggesting accrual-based profits outrunning actual cash generation. The business has funded its asset growth (51→79 Cr in two years) almost entirely through borrowings, not retained earnings — a pattern that historically ends poorly in commodity-adjacent industries during downturns. There is no dividend, no margin of safety, and no fortress balance sheet. Mr. Market is offering me this stock at a speculative price; I decline.
